title: JPA Transactions
summary: Group repository operations within a service transaction.

richText: Commit and rollback
A transaction groups database operations into one unit of work.
Commit keeps the changes. Rollback discards the uncommitted changes when the work fails.
Use a service transaction when several repository operations must succeed together.
A database transaction does not undo an email or an external HTTP request.
The service boundary
@Transactional marks a method whose database work should use a transaction.
With the usual Spring Boot JPA configuration, Boot configures a JPA transaction manager.
The default propagation joins an existing transaction or starts one when none exists.
Inherited repository write operations already have transaction settings. Separate repository calls are not automatically one service-level transaction.
A proxy is an object Spring puts around a bean to intercept method calls. Transaction handling uses this proxy by default.
Call the method through the injected Spring bean. A same-instance call to another annotated method bypasses the proxy and does not apply that method’s transaction settings.

example.title: Save two employees together
description: Use Employee and EmployeeRepository from the earlier JPA pages.
Call addPair through the injected HiringService bean, for example from another service or a controller.
explanation: The outer service transaction groups both saves.
If the work succeeds and commit succeeds, both changes are kept.
If a save throws a runtime exception that leaves the method, the transaction rolls back instead of keeping only the first employee.

richText: Rollback rules
By default, RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback. Checked exceptions do not.
Set rollbackFor when a checked exception must cause rollback.
Catching a failure and returning normally can allow a commit. Let the failure reach the transaction boundary when it should roll back.
Read-only transactions
@Transactional(readOnly=true) tells transaction infrastructure that the operation intends to read data.
It is an optimization hint. It is not a permission check or a portable guarantee that writes are rejected.
A transaction keeps a persistence context available while the service reads required entity data.
